title: Dynamic programming and shortest-path recurrences
summary: Recognize optimal substructure, write a one- and two-step recurrence, and turn it into a table with explicit complexity.
objectives: Fill a table and reconstruct a solution

sections.title: Lecture core · Optimal substructure
sections.body: Dynamic programming is useful when an optimal solution can be assembled from optimal solutions to smaller subproblems. Store each subproblem once so the same suffix or prefix is not recomputed exponentially many times.

sections.title: Textbook depth · One- and two-step recurrence
sections.body: For a path where a state can be reached from the previous one or two positions, a minimum-cost recurrence is $dp[i]=cost[i]+\min(dp[i-1],dp[i-2])$, with base cases stated separately. The exact indexing depends on whether cost is charged on entry, departure, or an edge; define it before computing.

math.explanation: The recurrence enumerates every allowed last jump. The minimum over those alternatives is the Bellman choice for the subproblem ending at i.

symbols.meaning: cost associated with position or transition

math.name: One- and two-step recurrence formula
math.purpose: Use it to make the one- and two-step recurrence claim operational; state its assumptions before applying it.

sections.title: Assessment habit · Table, recurrence, complexity
sections.body: A complete written answer should name the state, give the base cases, derive the recurrence from the final move, show enough table entries to demonstrate evaluation order, and state $O(n)$ time with $O(n)$ memory (or $O(1)$ extra memory if only the last two entries are retained).

sections.title: Bridge · Bellman recursion is a family resemblance
sections.body: Finite-horizon shortest path DP, MDP value iteration, and policy evaluation all reuse the idea of replacing a long plan with a local decision plus an optimal continuation. The state definition and boundary conditions determine whether the recurrence is correct.

examples.title: Table for jumps of one or two
steps: Let dp[0]=0, and let the costs of positions 1 through 4 be [1,4,2,7].
dp[1]=1. For position 2, dp[2]=4+$min(1,0)=4$. For position 3, dp[3]=2+$min(4,1)=3$.
For position 4, dp[4]=7+$min(3,4)=10$. The best predecessor of position 4 is position 3.
examples.answer: The table exposes the dependency order and makes a greedy mistake easy to detect.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why is a greedy nearest step not enough?
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The cheapest immediate move can lead to an expensive suffix. DP compares all allowed final moves after storing their optimal continuation costs.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What must be stated before a recurrence?
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Define what dp[i] means, when cost is charged, and the base cases. Without these, the same-looking recurrence can have an off-by-one or wrong-terminal-state error.
